en: PHIVOLCS maintains a six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone around Mayon Volcano to protect people from sudden explosive eruptions.
Living near Manila Bay requires knowing tsunami evacuation routes because the coast is vulnerable to earthquake-generated waves.
The wet season in Metro Manila increases mosquito breeding, making it crucial to clear stagnant water to prevent dengue.
Hikers climbing Mount Pulag must bring thick jackets because nighttime temperatures can drop to near freezing, risking hypothermia.
During heavy typhoons, the Cagayan River swells rapidly, so residents in its floodplains must evacuate to higher ground immediately.
Because the Philippines is near the equator, ultraviolet radiation is intense year-round, requiring daily sunscreen use to prevent skin damage.
Provinces facing the Pacific Ocean, like Eastern Samar, experience the most typhoons, requiring families to prepare emergency go-bags every rainy season.
Swimming in Laguna de Bay requires caution because nutrient runoff can cause harmful algal blooms that irritate the skin and eyes.
When Taal Volcano emits ashfall, residents must wear N95 masks to prevent fine volcanic particles from damaging their lungs.
Communities in the steep mountains of Benguet must avoid building houses near cliff edges to prevent fatal landslide accidents during heavy rains.
Snorkeling in Palawan's coral reefs requires wearing water shoes to prevent painful cuts from sharp corals and venomous sea urchins.
Metro Manila's dense concrete structures trap heat, making the urban heat island effect dangerous during summer, so staying hydrated is essential.
